system:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I plan and run the flights as a dispatcher, which includes deciding which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. I do want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Before and during a flight, outside people and devices report whether the load is ready, if the drone reaches its job points, and when it arrives.
The question: When several dispatchers plan at once for the same drone or the same busy site, what goes wrong today, and what should the service do when two plans want the same drone or the same site slot at the same time?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Can one drone be planned for two flights whose times overlap, and can a site (launch or landing place) take more than one drone at the same time? What are the limits?

Q4
The answer just before it: Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. My notes do not state whether one drone can be planned for two flights whose times overlap, so I don't know.
The question: When a site's take-off and landing places are all taken for the time you want, what should happen to your plan: refused, warned, or something else? And who sets the number of places a site has?

Q5
The answer just before it: I don't know what should happen to my plan, and I don't know who sets the number of places a site has.
The question: What do you check before you sign off a flight for departure, and what must be true for you to be allowed to sign it off?

Q6
The answer just before it: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies and along which way before signing off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight. My notes do not state what I check before I sign off a flight for departure or what must be true for me to be allowed to sign it off.
The question: You said you want help finding which of your drones could get to where a job starts. What makes a drone able or unable to get there (location, battery, range, load capacity, condition, airspace), and what should the service show you?

Q7
The answer just before it: Drones are of several models from different manufacturers that differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. Each drone has a home site, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. I don't know what the service should show me.
The question: The outside people and devices that report load readiness, job points reached, and arrival: who or what are they, how do their reports reach you, and what problems do you have with those reports (late, missing, duplicated, wrong order, from the wrong sender)?

Q8
The answer just before it: Reports come through relay stations because radio coverage is patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather. Because of this, reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. My notes do not state who or what the outside people and devices are.
The question: When reports arrive late, out of order, or twice, what do you need the service to do so that you still see the true state of a flight? And what should happen when no report arrives at all for a flight in the air?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know what I need the service to do when reports arrive late, out of order, or twice. My notes do not state what should happen when no report arrives at all for a flight in the air.
The question: What are all the things that can force you to change or call off a flight after you have planned it or signed it off, and what do you do in each case?

Q10
The answer just before it: I can call off a flight, and a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned and sudden closures, which are often amended during the day. My notes do not state all the things that can force me to change a flight or what I do in each case.
The question: What does a job consist of (start point, job points, load, time window, needed sensors, client), where do jobs come from, and are there differences between the kinds of work (parcel delivery, inspection, hospital logistics) that the service must handle?

Q11
The answer just before it: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. Drones fly along corridors between named sites. My notes do not state where jobs come from or what differences exist between the kinds of work the service must handle.
The question: Should the service let you plan or sign off a flight along a corridor that is closed, or through a prohibited zone, at the time the drone would be there? And when a closure is entered or amended later, what do you need to learn about your already planned and airborne flights?

Q12
The answer just before it: I don't know whether the service should let me plan or sign off a flight along a closed corridor or through a prohibited zone. My notes do not state what I need to learn about my already planned and airborne flights when a closure is entered or amended later.
The question: Is there anything else you know about your work, the flights, the sites, the drones, the reports, or what the service must not do, that you have not yet told me? Please tell me everything.

Q13
The answer just before it: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business, and we accept sharing airspace information because it comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone. Our drones are of several models from different manufacturers with different capacities, ranges, sensors, and charging connectors, and each has a home site with our own charging pads that are never lent to another company. The platform company runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours, and it occasionally crashes, which we accept for a few minutes of interruption. Finally, there are many things we do not want, such as software that plans routes or picks drones, billing or pricing, management reports, staff accounts inside the service, or alerts by e-mail, text message, or phone.
The question: Are the named sites your drones take off from and land at used only by your company, or do drones of other companies also use the same sites and their take-off and landing places? If shared, what may you learn about other companies' use of a site?

Q14
The answer just before it: Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, and these pads are never lent to another company. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I don't know whether drones of other companies use the same sites or what I may learn about other companies' use of a site.
The question: Roughly how many drones, sites, dispatchers and flights per day does your company have, and how quickly must you see a change (a new report, a closure, another dispatcher's plan) after it happens?

Q15
The answer just before it: I don't know how many drones, sites, dispatchers, or flights per day my company has. My notes do not state how quickly I must see a change after it happens.
The question: You said batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. What has that caused in practice, and what do you want the service to do about a drone's battery when you plan a flight and while it flies?

Q16
The answer just before it: My notes state that batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, but they do not state what this has caused in practice or what I want the service to do about a drone's battery when planning and flying.
The question: Who besides a dispatcher may plan, change, sign off or call off a flight, and may a technician or the airspace desk do any of those things or see your flights?

Q17
The answer just before it: I don't know who besides a dispatcher may plan, change, sign off, or call off a flight. My notes do not state whether a technician or the airspace desk may do any of those things or see my flights.
The question: For an inspection, the drone must visit points in a set order and return to the start. What does it mean for you if a point is reported out of order, skipped, or the arrival is reported at a different site than planned?

Q18
The answer just before it: My notes do not state what it means for me if a point is reported out of order, skipped, or if the arrival is reported at a different site than planned. I only know that inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started.
The question: When may you call off a flight: only before it leaves, or also while it is in the air? What happens to the drone and its load when a flight is called off or a closure hits it in the air?

Q19
The answer just before it: I am a dispatcher and can call off a flight, and a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. My notes do not state whether I may call off a flight only before it leaves or also while it is in the air. Furthermore, my notes do not state what happens to the drone and its load when a flight is called off or a closure hits it in the air.
The question: When you ask which of your drones could get to where a job starts, do you mean reachable along corridors that are open, within the drone's range, and fit for the job (load capacity, sensors)? What do you do if a drone is not at the start site?

Q20
The answer just before it: I am a dispatcher, and my company's policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, though I do want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. My notes do not state whether I mean reachable along open corridors, within range, and fit for the job, nor do they state what I do if a drone is not at the start site.
The question: When the server restarts or crashes for a few minutes while your drones fly, what must be intact when it comes back, and what should happen to reports and to your own actions that were sent during the interruption?

Q21
The answer just before it: My notes state that the platform runs on a single server which is updated and restarted during working hours, while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes, and we accept a few minutes of interruption. My notes do not state what must be intact when the server comes back or what should happen to reports and actions sent during the interruption.
The question: With no staff accounts or passwords inside the service, how do you expect the service to know that an action comes from your company and from a dispatcher, and must it record which person signed off a flight?

Q22
The answer just before it: I don't know how the service knows that an action comes from my company and from a dispatcher without staff accounts or passwords inside the service. My notes do not state whether the service must record which person signed off a flight.
The question: Please list every single thing your notes say the companies do not want in this service, and anything your notes say about laws or rules that apply.

Q23
The answer just before it: My company does not want management or analytical reports, exports, and dashboards beyond day-to-day operations, or logging in through our own corporate identity systems. We also do not want several languages, any guarantee of meeting regulations, any compliance audit, data-retention or deletion features, backups, high availability, or spreading the service over several servers. We reject accounts and passwords inside the service, alerts to staff by e-mail, text message, or phone, software that plans routes or picks drones, and flying drones remotely through the service. Finally, we do not want weather information, billing or pricing of the work, or signing up new companies through the service. The relevant rules are the EU drone operation rules, including geographical zones and operator responsibilities, the EU U-space rules, including airspace information and flight authorisation, and the GDPR for personal data of staff.
The question: Do several dispatchers work on the same flight or only each on their own, and what must never happen when two of you act on the same drone, flight or site place at the same moment?

Q24
The answer just before it: My notes state that several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. However, my notes do not state whether several dispatchers work on the same flight or only each on their own. I also do not know what must never happen when two of us act on the same drone, flight, or site place at the same moment.
The question: May a flight leave before its load is reported ready or before you have signed it off, and how do you learn that a flight has actually left, reached each job point, and arrived?
